title: Basic Fonio
author: Pierre Thiam
desc: A cup of fonio washed until the water runs clear, then steamed in a cheesecloth-lined basket or boiled two minutes and rested — two ways, both Thiam’s.
longDesc: The base recipe for every fonio dish in this collection. The grain is submerged in warm water, swished and drained repeatedly until the water runs clear. For the traditional steamer method it goes into a cheesecloth-lined basket over simmering salted water for about 15 minutes, is fluffed, sprinkled with a few tablespoons of salted water and steamed 5 to 10 minutes more. For the stovetop method, 1 cup of water and a tablespoon of salt boil; the washed fonio is stirred in, covered, cooked on low about 2 minutes, then left off the heat 5 to 10 minutes. A cup of dry fonio makes about 4 cups.
ingredients: Stovetop method: 1 cup water and 1 tbsp salt — in the method, not the ingredient list
Steamer method: a few tablespoons of salted water for the second steam
Optional: a little butter or oil to keep the grains separate
equipment: Steamer basket lined with damp cheesecloth, or medium pot with lid
steps: Wash the fonio: submerge it in warm water, swish with your fingers, pour off and repeat several times until the water runs clear. Drain well.

Steamer method: set the fonio in a steamer basket lined with damp cheesecloth over simmering salted water. Cover and steam about 15 minutes. Fluff with a fork, drizzle a few tablespoons of salted water over and steam another 5 to 10 minutes, until the grains are completely tender. Fluff.

Stovetop method: boil 1 cup of water in a medium pot, stir in the washed fonio and the tablespoon of salt, cover tightly, reduce to low and cook about 2 minutes, until the water is just absorbed. Turn off the heat, fluff gently — especially the wetter bottom — cover and let sit 5 to 10 minutes, until tender.
chefTips: The washing is the step: the water should run clear.
Steaming in a basket is called ‘the traditional way’ on the JBF page.
Thiam also says a rice cooker works at a 1:1 ratio of fonio to water.
Butter or oil in the cooking water keeps the grains separate.
commonMistakes: Over-stirring the stovetop fonio while it rests.
servedWith: Any mafé, yassa or grilled meat
healthBenefits: Fonio is gluten-free and contains methionine and cysteine.
Rich in iron compared with most cereals.
culturalNote: The JBF page gives no historical or cultural information about fonio or Senegal — only that it is healthy and gluten-free, and that steaming in a basket is the traditional way. That absence is recorded: the ‘fonio revival’ framing comes from other sources in this set.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Basic Fonio’. Byline: Pierre Thiam. James Beard Foundation page, no date printed (footer ‘Copyright ©2025’). Reprinted from ‘Senegal: Modern Senegalese Recipes from the Source to the Bowl’ by Pierre Thiam with Jennifer Sit. Yield: 4 cups. SINGLE-PASS on wording, TWO-PASS on every figure (both passes returned identical quantities and times).
FLAGGED OMISSION on both passes: the stovetop method additionally calls for 1 cup of water and 1 tablespoon of salt, neither of which is in the printed ingredient list.

Corroborated by the WBUR printing (19 October 2015, ‘Makes about 4 cups’): same times, same cue ‘until the grains are completely tender’, plus Thiam’s note that quinoa can substitute and that a rice cooker works at 1:1 fonio to water.

UNRECONCILED within Thiam’s own work: this recipe says about 2 minutes covered then a 5–10 minute rest; a Lake Isle blog post on jollof fonio says add to boiling water, cover and simmer for five minutes, then turn off the heat and leave covered two minutes more. A Splendid Table printing says about 5 minutes covered then 2 more off the heat (SEN065). Neither is picked.
Cues in short fragments: ‘until the grains are completely tender’; ‘until the water is just absorbed’; ‘until tender’.
Prep/rest/cook times are the sum of the printed ranges for the stovetop method taken at its midpoint.
